paragraphs.text: Just now, when those honoured before us [?] by the grace of God sounded forth their godly strains, we too were all with you, united in the word of truth. We learned the same things, rejoiced in the same things and delighted in them together. No one who understands what is good would take any joy for himself; he gives it all to the glory of God. Whoever agrees with the speaker shares in fellowship with the Giver, for in praising the speaker he worships the One who is preached. Our fathers, whose ways are free of envy, have taught us this, and above all our father here. He is head of all the fathers, sits on the honoured throne above them all, and has a mind clear and pure of jealousy. He himself first composes the spiritual and artful strain and sounds it in everyone's ears: "Would that all the people of God were prophets!" Such is the spirit that glorifies its Lord: it counts the words and virtues of others as its own. If anyone disparages the words of others, he sets himself against the one who gave the grace, not against the one who received it. The mind shows in the face. Look at our common father: see how cheerful his face is and how sweetly his eyes rest on us who speak and on you who listen. When you see someone with his face cast down, recognize the deceit in his mind. When the countenance droops, know that the heart is plotting deceit. As Scripture says, "Whoever winks with the eye plots deceit."

Christ is glorified and the world is enlightened, while the one whose mind is set on evil sits heart-stricken, his liver burning, wounded to the depths. Since we have met with the freedom from envy of our holy and pure father, we have learned without guile, and without envy let us give. So let us take up the beginning of the sequence we were following yesterday. We left it off because of the many different thoughts that came flowing in from every side. Our desire was to explain a little of the beginning of the Gospel, and we do not know how the contest [?] that arose between us and the heretics turned us away from it. Yet we did not wander from one subject into others; we kept our attention on the same matter and the same meaning. Christ is glorified, and the war against those who fight Christ is set in order. Let every disease be cast out! Let those be put to shame who today keep the feast of stumbling-blocks and phantoms, a bare name empty of the righteousness of truth.

Those who have put on Christ keep Passover with the Jews; those clothed with Christ share in fellowship with those who fight against Christ. I call them "clothed with Christ" because of the name they profess. But what fellowship can light have with darkness? What agreement can the Jews have with Christ? What equality is there between the table of Christ and the [?] table of the Jews? The children of godliness keep Passover with dogs. They ought to be singing hymns with the angels, and instead they howl with dogs. The godly person praises with the angels: "I will give thanks to you, Lord, with my whole heart; before your angels I will sing psalms to you." The godly person gives glory with the angels, but whoever corrupts the ordinances of the Church howls through the feast with dogs. These are not words of insult but of truth and reproof. Hear Paul, the great preacher, who says: "Beware of the dogs, beware of the evil workers."

They have taken up the heavenly lamps, yet they keep the lamp-lighting vigil with the Jews. They receive the Lamb of God and keep the Pascha, yet they slaughter sheep with the Jews. Oh, what folly! The shadow seeks to destroy the truth, and those who have laid hold of the truth run after shadows. Why do you light a lamp with the Jews? Is it not so that your light [?] may be put out from the Gospel? Whoever shelters a rebel and lends a rebel a hand will suffer the same punishment with him. Hear David: "If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you threw in your lot with adulterers." Would that it were only with adulterers, and not with those who fight against God! Adultery and fornication are foul and loathsome names and deeds, and they deserve eternal torments. Yet these are sins of human beings against human beings, of servants against fellow servants, but to sin against God surpasses every sin. An offence committed against a master is graver than one against a fellow servant. In the same way, when someone fights against God, that sin is more grievous than all other sins. Why do you, a child of godliness, keep feast [?] with the children of perdition? Suppose you saw someone under the king's punishment, banished [?] from the royal presence. Would you want to strike up a friendship with him? Would you not rather break off any friendship you already had, so as to escape punishment yourself?

Let us see where the Jews stand and what the condition of the Christians is. Hear the holy Gospel: "Whoever believes in the Son," it says, "receives eternal life, and whoever disobeys the Son will not see life." The living are keeping the feast with the lifeless! What good did the Jews ever devise? What order of godliness did they keep uncorrupted, that you should take fine customs from them and add them to the Church as a needful foundation? Do you not hear the prophet saying, "You, house of Israel, have been perverse all your youth and have lied against the truth"? For they denied godliness and sold it, because they did not understand. They did not even keep their wine pure. Is that not the very first charge the prophet Isaiah brings against them? "Your merchants," he says, "mix water with wine." Would that the schismatics of today mixed water with wine, and not God with creatures! See how the prophets' accusation against the Jews stands in writing, and the apostles also preach it openly. Hear Paul, the great preacher, writing to the Thessalonians: "I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that you suffered the same things from your own countrymen as the church of God did from the Jews. They killed the Lord Jesus and their own prophets and persecuted us; they are displeasing to God and hostile to all people." Will you make yourself a partner of those who lie under punishments beyond measure? To such people Isaiah says, "That is your portion, and that is the lot of your inheritance."

I would like to learn from them why they keep the feast at all, and with what hope. They do away with repentance, so why do they perform this vain, empty and senseless service? They live without hope of repentance, though they need repentance more than anyone. They are covered with sores, and they deny the physician. They go about under the name of Cathari, that is, "the pure," yet they have purity neither in body nor in mind. Nothing so angers God, provokes him to wrath and makes a person liable to great torments as calling oneself by a holy name. Even if someone were pure of every sin, he ought to count himself among the sinners. Hear the holy John: "Little children, if we sin, we are not of God"; and again, "Whoever does evil is not of God." Having given the counsel not to sin, he then brings forward the truth. The same man who said, "Whoever sins is not of God," comes down lower still and says, "If we say that we have not sinned, we lie." He gave the counsel to be watchful without denying the remedy [?]. He kept his eye on the teaching of truth, but he also saw how easily the mind slips and stumbles. Now, however, the enemies of godliness keep feasts and demand exactness in works [?], while they themselves have strayed from all firm ground.

I too would like to raise such matters with you who love Christ, and to show that this opposition is pointless and its opinion empty. When someone departs from the order of the Church, he does not stay in harbour [?]. Error seizes him and carries him off, like the currents of rivers that pour into the sea. What do Pascha and the feast signify? What is accomplished on the day of the feast? Are not the sufferings and resurrection of Christ preached, salvation proclaimed to the world, and every soul enlightened by the divine Word? Then how can this be? Do we hold that seal and pledge of godliness on only one day of the year? Is not every Sunday the Church's Pascha? Is that sacrifice one thing and this another? Is the splendour of the mysteries one thing at Pascha and another on Sunday, on Wednesday and on Friday? As often as you celebrate the memorial of Christ's sufferings, you keep Pascha. In former times the slaughter of lambs took place once a year, but the sacrifice of Christ is offered every day. That is why the Life-giver made it clear that the mystery is not bound to times and days, or months and years, when he said to his disciples: "As often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim my death." Who, then, keeps that feast? Whoever performs that same mystery keeps Pascha continually.

"But if the mysteries are performed continually," they say, "what need is there for a new feast?" There is great need. God has often given such things to console our human nature in its weakness. God's mystery always stands unmoved and firm, and so do the altar, the priests, the offerings, the services and everything performed in his name. But God saw human weakness, how it is mingled with earthly things and tangled up in all kinds of defilement. So through the holy apostles he provided a means to meet it: the feast of Pascha. Someone may be entangled in sin at all times and nailed down by earthly needs, unwilling to look toward the light of godliness. At least at the name of the feast he may turn his eyes, and through the memory of the life-giving sufferings prepare himself to partake of the holy things.

Feasts exist so that many may gather in one place, but for the saints every day is a feast. What is the saints' feast? To bless God. So whoever blesses God continually keeps an unceasing feast. Hear David saying, "I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall continually be in my mouth." Whoever praises without ceasing is always keeping feast. The names of Pascha, of [?], and of all the general feasts point to the gathering of many into one place. They exist to enlighten the darkened, bring back those who have strayed, straighten crooked ways, raise the dead and buried, and in every way build up the members of Christ for all. It is no wonder that those who split away from the Church should also separate themselves from its feast, for "if they had been of us, they would have remained with us." Let the faithful rebuke the corrupting feast, and let our feast shine in its own season. This is not because grace is subject to times, but so that all order and arrangement may be planted in the Church. Let us now return to the sequence of our discourse. Let us speak and preach without counting the preaching as our own. We do it in service to our holy father, paying the debt of the paternal discourse that has been delayed [?]. I say this so that no one unaware of the circumstances may blame us, as though we were seizing for ourselves the time that belongs to our father's teaching. We do what we are commanded, and we necessarily follow our father's will.

Yesterday, brothers, our task was to proclaim and discuss a little of the theology at the beginning of the Gospel, and to show what purpose the words reveal. John says, "In the beginning was the Word." He did not say, "In the beginning was the Son," or "the Only-begotten." He made the hearers' minds secure, lest the mind, unable to grasp theology, should defile the divine begetting with human notions. Among us, whenever there is talk of birth, notions of father and mother come in, along with the grossness of the body and the causes of passions. So he first hides the name "Son" and presents the title "Word," so that by the name "Word" he might make plain that the Begetter and the begetting are free of passion. Let me say it once more: he calls him "Word" to show that the begetting is not subject to passions.

"And was with God," he says, to make plain that the honour is undivided. He said, "was with God," and showed that he is God. Then he also brings in his work as Creator: "All things were made through him." So let the vain labour of the disputers be refuted. From the expressions "through him" and "by him" they try to construct a lessening of the Only-begotten's honour.

Perhaps someone will say: "Suppose the schismatics demanded an answer, and could not say themselves what 'through him' means and what 'by him' means. You who belong to the Church, explain what 'through him' is and what 'by him' is." The divine Scriptures do not use the language of the technical schools, nor do they serve the constructions of the human mind. They are not Aristotelian rules or Platonic distinctions. They are simple faith, without deceit or cunning and full of great freedom. When Scripture says "through him" and "by him," it means "from him." "All things were made through him": what does "through him" mean? Exactly the same as "from him." When it says, "Let the waters bring forth," and "Let the earth bring forth," does it call the water and the earth creator? When Paul says, "The first man was from the earth, made of dust," is the earth the creator? And when he says, "Man was not from woman, but woman from man," is the man the woman's [creator]? You see that "from him" does not always refer to the creator; it can also refer to some material in between. Clearly, then, saying "by him" and "through him" of the Life-giver does not mean that he used some material. It means that he brought what did not exist into existence and called what is not into being. God's will is not like the material and timber of craftsmen, nor is it God's essence. His works do not come forth from God's essence; his will brings what is not into being and what does not exist into existence. He wills, and all things come to be; he nods, and all things obey.

So when Scripture says "from him," it means "from the will of the Father"; and when it says "through him" and "by him," it means "from the power of the Son." Some seek excuses for sin, and blessed Paul takes this excuse away from them when he says: "Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor? Or who has lent to him, that he should be repaid? For all things are from him and through him." If "through him" showed some inferiority and "from him" a superior honour, how can he say both here of one and the same person? Does he mix things that cannot be mixed? Of whom do they think "all things are from him and through him" was said: of the Father or of the Son? If of the Father, then look: they have brought the Father down to "by him" and "through him" as well, if "by him" means servitude. And if they took "through him" as servitude, it would be a gross insult to say "from him," "by him" and "through him" of the Father, since one person cannot be both master and servant. Or was it said of the Son? Then look: it is not only "through him" and "by him" but also "from him," and one person cannot be both a servant and the author of the work himself. To clear away our fancies, he joined both expressions in one person, so that you may learn that words do not divide the nature of God. "From him," "by him," "through him" and "in him" were all said of one and the same: sometimes of the Father, sometimes of the Son.

They keep repeating "by whom" and "through him," and on that basis they ascribe servitude, lowliness and inferiority to the Son. So I must gather some words of the prophets and set them before you. Blessed Joseph overcame every evil by his humility. While he was in prison, he saw Pharaoh's eunuchs there with sad faces; their looks revealed the gloom in their hearts. "Why are your faces sad today?" he asked. "We have had a dream," they said, "and there is no one to interpret it for us." And what did blessed Joseph answer? "Tell me the dream." He did not say that its interpretation is "from God," but "through God." If they are right, are you the lord, and is God the servant? Is the interpretation not "through him"? He ought to have said it was "from God." Do you speak through God and by God, or does God speak through you and by you? So do not be enslaved to the weakness of words; listen to the grace of God and to the Old Testament. "These are the words and commandments that Moses, the servant of the Lord, commanded at the Lord's command" — that the commands were through Moses [?]. Pay attention: "These are," it says, "the words and commandments that Moses commanded." It did not say "God through Moses," but "Moses through God."

He said "Word," called him "God," and named him "Creator." Little by little he gently approaches the title "only-begotten Son." "All things," he says, "were made by him": he proclaims him Creator. "And without him nothing was made" of the things that were made, though this does not include the uncreated nature. Do you remember the first words we spoke, that Scripture speaks with reference to the matters in hand, alluding to them? The disciples of the schismatics, who wage war against the Holy Spirit, use "all things were made by him" to blaspheme the Holy Spirit too. "All things were made by him" means everything that was made, not the uncreated nature. When the Life-giver says, "All who came before me were thieves and robbers," will you slander Moses as a thief and Isaiah as a robber? Surely he calls "thieves and robbers" those the words were about.

"All things were made by him, and without him nothing was made that was made. In him was life." He said that he is the Word, called him God, said that he was with God, and named him Creator. Now he calls him Life as well, for the Creator is surely also the Life-giver. One cannot be Creator without giving living power to creatures. He was Life because he has the grace that gives life and light. Everything that has been established needs life, and what lives needs light; no one can enjoy light without life. That is why he adds, in the same place, "He was life, and the life was the light of men."

He has shown the creative power that gives life and light. Then he says, "There was a man sent from God, whose name was John." Where he speaks of God, he uses "was"; where he speaks of the man, he uses "came to be." "He came as a witness, to bear witness to the light, so that all might be established through him." Here the schismatic finds an excuse. "You see," he says, "that 'through him' signifies servitude, for God becomes trusted even through the prophets." But consider: human nature is indeed subject to the law and to service of the Lord, yet here "by whom" signifies no servitude. It signifies the inspiration and preaching of the prophets, for the witness to the light bore witness willingly, not unwillingly. But if they persist in harshness and obstinacy [?] and take "by whom" and "through him" as a mark of servitude, let them hear Paul, who says: "God is faithful, by whom you were called into obedience to his Son." Here "by whom" and "through him" no longer run from the Son to the Father, but from the Father to the Son.

"He was in the world," it says, "and came into the world." Having said that he came into the world, he adds, "He was in this world, and came into the world," so that no one should imagine a change of place in the incorporeal One. Then how do they say, "whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world"? The sending shows no change of place; it shows the manifestation of the divine plan. Hear how this can be. Where does wheat appear from? Where do wine and oil come from? Is it not from the earth? Why then did God say, "Behold, I am sending you wheat and wine and oil"? The wheat that is "sent" does not come from heaven; Scripture shows the sending by the appearing of the crop. Yet you suppose that the incorporeal Creator, Being from true Being, Existent from true Existent, was sent by a change of place and not by the manifestation of the divine plan? If the Son was sent from place to place, then the Father remained only up above and the Son came down only here below, and the Son was not in heaven, nor [the Father] on earth. Think this through carefully. Suppose you are enslaved to the word and understand the Son's sending as though he were separated from the one who sent him. Then the one sent from heaven would necessarily be only on earth and cut off from heaven, and the sender would not be on earth but confined to heaven. Who is so impious and lawless, so ready to sharpen a tongue that fights against God, as to confine the Father to heaven alone and shut the Son up on earth alone?

Do you want to learn true theology, not spoken at random but attested by Scripture: that the Son was sent and yet remained on high, that he ascended into heaven and yet is with us? These are not my words but those of the Life-giver himself. "Whom the Father," he says, "sanctified and sent." This makes it seem as though he were separated from the one who sent him. Then how does the one who was sent say, "I am in the Father and the Father is in me"? And again, "The Father who sent me is with me"? If he is with you, then you were not sent alone; you were sent together with him. If you understand his sending as a bodily sending, how can he say of the sender, the Father, "I am in the Father and the Father is in me," and again, "He who sent me is with me"? Someone hearing "He who sent me is with me" might suppose this meant some power acting on him, and not the Father himself. To prevent this, he clarifies the word in another place: "The Father," he says, "who dwells in me does the works." He says "who dwells in me," not "who works in me by influences."

He came from heaven and remained there in heaven; he ascended from the earth and was not separated from the earth. These are not my words; hear the Lord himself: "I am going up to the Father," he says, "and I will send you the Holy Spirit." "I am going up" shows distance, while "I will send" shows that there is no distance. So that no one should think his ascension in the body was a change in the Godhead, he commands his disciples: "Go, make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; and behold, I am with you always, to the end of the world." What does "I am with you" mean? We recognize the Word by his very voice: he spoke in the prophets then, and now he works mighty deeds. "Go and make disciples of all nations, and behold, I am with you." Who said this? Clearly the one who spoke through the prophet Haggai: "Now be strong, Zerubbabel, says the Lord, and let the hands of my people be strong, and work on my house, for I am with you, and my Spirit abides in your midst."

God is everywhere and with all believers: the Father is in the midst of believers, the Son is in the midst of believers, and the Holy Spirit too is in the midst of believers. How is the Father in the midst of believers? Hear the prophet: "Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion; exult and delight with all your heart, for the Lord has taken away your wrongs and saved you from the hands of your enemies. He will reign in your midst; the Lord will reign in your midst, and you will see evil no more." Here the Father is shown reigning in the midst of believers. And the Son? "Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them." The Father is in the midst, the Son is in the midst, and the Holy Spirit also is in the midst: "For I am with you, says the Lord Almighty, and the Spirit stood in your midst." Why do you divide what is indivisible? Why do you tear apart what cannot be torn apart? I mean the body that he united to himself; no one dares say that it is separate. I know that I once spoke on this same subject. But we must not look back to what was said before and abandon teaching when the time is right. For [?] this is what words are for: not to pass over the same things, but never to depart from them.

The disciples of the heretics say: “See how the Son shares an equal-honoured fellowship with us: ‘I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’ See how the Son calls the Father his God.” Now, before anything else, we must observe this: the only-begotten nature, the impassible essence, the incorruptible and unchangeable power, took up his own creation and united the body to himself. He did not himself descend into lowliness; rather, he raised its lowliness to greatness. And see how he carries out a heavenly exchange with humanity. One who makes an exchange both gives and receives: he took a body from us and gave us the Spirit from himself. You, whose God and Lord he is, would not dare to call God Father if you had not received the Spirit from him. In the same way, the Son would not call the Father his God if he had not taken a body from you. The Life-giver knew that his Father and our Father are not Father in the same way, and that his God and our God are not God in the same way. So he distinguishes the names: “to my Father and to your Father,” for mine is of one kind and yours of another; “and to my God and to your God,” for your God is God in one way and mine in another. “Because of the body taken from you, the Father became my God; and because of the Spirit taken from me, he became God and Father of the world. I, the Son, could not call the Father God if I had not taken the body. Nor could you in any way call God Father if you had not received the Spirit.” And Paul bears witness: “Because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son, who cries out in your hearts, ‘Abba, Father.’” I ascend to my Father by nature and to your Father by grace; to your God by this nature, and to my God by this body.

John says, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father.” “Why,” they ask, “did he not mention the Spirit? Why did he speak [?] of the Son of God and say nothing of the Spirit?” Brothers, we must understand that the mystical doctrines are one thing and public preaching is another. In their preaching the apostles proclaimed the faith, but they handed down the truth in the mysteries. They could not trust dull hearers, and so they could not lay out the doctrine of the Trinity openly. Consider what Christ says to the apostles: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.” The apostles were born of the Jews and were worshippers of God, raised in a faith that worshipped God. They went about with Christ, saw the signs with their own eyes and beheld God the Word in the flesh. Yet even they could not bear to hear everything at once. How then could the apostles reveal the doctrine of the economy straight away to those who came from the gentiles? These had only just been freed from temples, blood, idols and many gods, and some were not yet free.

The fighter against the Spirit says: “Everywhere in the Scriptures I find the Father and the Son mentioned and the Spirit passed over in silence. First of all there is the Life-giver himself: ‘No one knows the Father except the Son, and no one knows the Son except the Father.’ Did he say ‘the Holy Spirit’? ‘No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son.’ He did not join the Spirit with the Father and the Son. How then can one count as belonging to the same Godhead someone who is not able to know the Father?” If the Son’s knowing here has sharpened your tongue to blaspheme the Spirit, what will you do if you see it said elsewhere that the Spirit knows the Father, with no mention of the Son? “No one has ascended into heaven, and no one knows the Father except the Son”: these are the Life-giver’s words. And the same voice speaks in Paul, for he says, “If you seek proof of Christ, who speaks in me.” What, then, does the voice of Christ say through Paul? “No one knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man; so also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God.” If you thrust the Spirit away in that passage, you must cast the Son aside in this one. But if the Son is not separated here, the Spirit is not divided there. There is another point as well. Sometimes Scripture mentions the Father alone and says nothing of the Son and the Spirit. Sometimes it mentions the Son alone and says nothing of the Father and the Spirit. And sometimes it mentions the Spirit alone and says nothing of the Father and the Son. Many other times it mentions the Father and the Son and says nothing of the Spirit, or mentions the Son and the Spirit and says nothing of the Father. Where it mentions the Father, does that mean it is silent about the Son?

The apostles once asked Christ, “Lord, teach us to pray.” He taught them the prayer and said, “Pray like this: Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name,” and so on, line by line, to the end of the prayer. Nowhere in it does he mention either himself or the Spirit. Here the Father alone is mentioned, and the glory of the Son and the Spirit goes unspoken. He was not denying anything. He kept silent about the Spirit and the Son for the time being because it was helpful, and for a mystical purpose. “Our Father who art in heaven”: here the Father alone is mentioned. But elsewhere the Life-giver himself, who taught the disciples to pray to the Father alone, says something else. See what it is: “Whatever you ask of me, I will do for you.” Here he makes no mention of the Father. He was not denying the Father; he was declaring his own dignity, equal in honour. Elsewhere Scripture mentions the Spirit alone and says nothing of the Father and the Son: “John baptized with water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit.” In the Holy Spirit alone? Then what clear tradition of the mystery does he give? “Baptize them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” Again, it speaks of the Father and the Son and is silent about the Spirit: “There is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.” For Paul was not speaking about doctrine at that point; he was doing away with the many gods. Learn this, and you will find the solution. As the Life-giver says, “Search the Scriptures,” not “search your own reasonings.” Do not trust the fancies of your reasonings; listen to Scripture: “The reasonings of mortals are timid, and their minds unsteady.” And again the Saviour says, “that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom you have sent”—and he is silent about the Spirit. Elsewhere Scripture speaks of the Father and the Spirit and is silent about the Son, as in the testimony quoted above: “Go in and work in my house, says the Lord Almighty, for I am with you, and my Spirit abides among you.” Where is the Son here? For he says, “I and my Spirit.” And elsewhere Paul mentions the Son and the Spirit and is silent about the Father: “Neither dogs, nor fornicators, nor thieves, nor drunkards, nor slanderers will inherit the kingdom of God. And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God.” Where is the Father here? “Search the Scriptures,” he says, “and do not search your own reasonings.”

Let us also state some plain facts that expose the transgression of the heretics. The apostle says, “The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit, for they seem folly to him.” The gentile is not scandalized, because he counts the preaching as folly; it is the Jew who is scandalized at Christ. And what does Paul say about this? “We preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to the Jews and folly to the gentiles.” Why does the gentile count the preaching as folly? Tell him that God made Christ as one of the creatures, and he does not argue with you; he says, “The Creator was able to do it.” Tell him that Christ was begotten, and he mocks and counts the word as foolishness. “Would God be begotten,” he says, “when his nature is free of passions?” Notice whose company the heretics share. The gentiles disparage the doctrine of the begetting as foolishness. And you divide and distort the begetting, and in place of the begetting you bring in a creature. You are found to be scandalized along with the Jews and to count the preaching as foolishness along with the gentiles. But we, brothers, are not heretics. We do not find the mystery unbearable; we are enlightened by faith.

You see that God is preached in the persons of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The prophets glorified the mystery before the mystery itself came, and will you distort the mystery that comes from prophecy? God spoke through the prophets as if from one person, and with it he presented knowledge of the Son and of the Spirit. And lest anyone think the apostles preached something new later, God shows that the matter is certain by saying something like this through the prophet Joel: “It shall come to pass in the last days, says God.” Notice that steadfast souls and attentive minds are needed here, so as not to forget the divine preaching. “And it shall come to pass in the last days, says God, that I will pour out of my Spirit on all flesh.” For the moment he spoke only of himself and of the Spirit, but he will go on to make the Son known as well. And what does he do? It was not yet the time for preaching or for open doctrine but for hidden mysteries. So he puts forward an intermediate figure [?], like a parable woven together, and weaves in many words, and at the end he presents knowledge of the Son. Making that knowledge plain might have given an occasion for sin to those who could not understand how things stood. So for the time being he speaks only of himself and the Spirit: “I will pour out of my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams.” And see how, while he is still speaking of himself and the Spirit, he gently presents knowledge of the Son as well: “And I will give signs in the heavens above and on the earth below, blood and fire and vapour of smoke. The sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes.” Is that day not yours, then, but another Lord’s? For you speak as if announcing good news about another Lord. If you are the God who is speaking, and you pour out your own Spirit, how can you announce good news about another Lord? Clearly, he calls the Son, who is from him, Lord: “before the day of the Lord comes, which is great and manifest.” The first coming took place in meekness and quietness, so he does not speak of that one. He speaks of the great and manifest coming, whose glory is plain to see.

And what follows in the passage? “And it shall be,” he says, “that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved.” He did not say, “whoever calls on my name shall be saved.” And so that the victory of the truth may not seem forced [?], I will set Paul before you as a witness. Which name shall we call on, and be saved? Paul answers—Paul, the tongue of truth, the interpreter of the prophets’ oracles: “Is he the God of the Jews only, and not of the gentiles also? Yes, of the gentiles also. For God is one, and he justifies the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through the same faith.” And elsewhere: “The same God is generous to all who call on him; and everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved.”

Now to make it plain that he applies the saying to Christ: the prophecy says, “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved,” and the apostle explains, “How shall they call on one in whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe in one in whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe in one of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without someone to preach? And how shall they preach unless they are sent? As it is written, How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of peace, who bring good news of good things!” He has shown himself, he has shown the Holy Spirit, and he has shown the Son. At the beginning of the prophecy he foretold things about himself and the Spirit; in the same way, at the end he seals the meaning of the prophecy with the Son. “For from Mount Zion,” he says, “shall come the one who is saved, and those who bring good news, whom the Lord has called to himself.” By “those who bring good news” he means the evangelists, who were called by the Lord: “Jesus called the twelve apostles and gave them authority over demons and unclean spirits.” And elsewhere, to show the royal and divine dignity of the Holy Spirit, Scripture says that the Spirit spoke about Paul and Barnabas: “Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I am about to call them.” So much on this point.

May these words enlighten the believers, and may they lead our opponents to feel shame and turn back. No great effort is needed: be put to shame by the word, and receive salvation. God once threatened the people of Jerusalem through the prophet, saying, “Behold, I will destroy them and bring them to nothing.” And when the Lord saw that their hearts had repented, the Lord said to the man of God, “Do you see how they were ashamed? I will not destroy them.” Through the prayers of the holy fathers, may they turn back, may we be established, and may the Church be glorified in Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
